{{Short description|Branch of the mathematical field of graph theory}}
{{about|the study of graph embeddings|graphs in the plane with crossings|topological graph}}
[[File:Pappus-graph-animation.webm|thumb|Animation detailing the embedding of the [[Pappus graph]] and associated map in the torus]]

In [[mathematics]], '''topological graph theory''' is a branch of [[graph theory]]. It studies the [[Graph embedding|embedding of graphs]] in [[Surface (topology)|surface]]s, [[linkless embedding|spatial embeddings of graphs]], and [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graphs]] as [[topological space]]s.<ref>{{cite book |first1=J.L. |last1=Gross |author2-link=Thomas W. Tucker |first2=T.W. |last2=Tucker |title=Topological Graph Theory |publisher=Dover |orig-date=1987 |date=2012 |isbn=978-0-486-41741-7 |url={{GBurl|6HmA_x0dL9oC|pg=PR9}}}}</ref> It also studies [[immersion (mathematics)|immersions]] of graphs.

Embedding a graph in a surface means that we want to draw the graph on a surface, a [[sphere]] for example, without two [[edge (graph theory)|edge]]s intersecting. A basic embedding problem often presented as a [[mathematical puzzle]] is the [[three utilities problem]]. Other applications can be found in printing [[electronic circuit]]s where the aim is to print (embed) a circuit (the graph) on a [[circuit board]] (the surface) without two connections crossing each other and resulting in a [[short circuit]].

== Graphs as topological spaces ==
{{see also|Graph (topology)|Graph homology}}

To an [[undirected graph]] we may associate an [[abstract simplicial complex]] ''C'' with a single-element set per vertex and a two-element set per edge. The geometric realization |''C''| of the complex consists of a copy of the [[unit interval]] [0,1] per edge, with the endpoints of these [[interval (mathematics)|intervals]] glued together at vertices. In this view, embeddings of graphs into a surface or as [[Subdivision (graph theory)|subdivisions]] of other graphs are both instances of topological embedding, [[Homeomorphism (graph theory)|homeomorphism of graphs]] is just the specialization of topological [[homeomorphism]], the notion of a [[connected graph]] coincides with [[connected space|topological connectedness]], and a connected graph is a [[tree (graph theory)|tree]] [[if and only if]] its [[fundamental group]] is trivial.

Other simplicial complexes associated with graphs include the [[Whitney complex]] or ''clique complex'', with a set per [[Clique (graph theory)|clique]] of the graph, and the ''matching complex'', with a set per [[Matching (graph theory)|matching]] of the graph (equivalently, the clique complex of the complement of the [[line graph]]). The matching complex of a [[complete bipartite graph]] is called a ''[[chessboard complex]]'', as it can be also described as the complex of sets of nonattacking rooks on a chessboard.<ref>{{cite journal |last1= Shareshian |first1=John |author2-link=Michelle L. Wachs |last2=Wachs |first2=Michelle L. |title = Torsion in the matching complex and chessboard complex |arxiv = math.CO/0409054 |journal=[[Advances in Mathematics]]
|volume=212 |issue=2 |orig-date=2004 |date=2007 |pages=525–570 |doi=10.1016/j.aim.2006.10.014 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

== Example studies ==
[[John Hopcroft]] and [[Robert Tarjan]]<ref>{{cite journal|title = Efficient planarity testing|journal = Journal of the ACM|volume = 21|issue = 4|year = 1974|pages = 549–568|doi = 10.1145/321850.321852 |last1 = Hopcroft|first1 = John|last2 = Tarjan|first2 = Robert E.|author-link1 = John Hopcroft|author-link2 = Robert Tarjan|hdl = 1813/6011|s2cid = 6279825|url = https://ecommons.cornell.edu/bitstream/1813/6011/1/73-165.pdf|hdl-access = free}}</ref> derived a means of [[planarity testing|testing the planarity]] of a graph in time linear to the number of edges.  Their algorithm does this by constructing a graph embedding which they term a "palm tree".  Efficient planarity testing is fundamental to [[graph drawing]].

[[Fan Chung]] et al<ref>{{cite journal|title = Embedding Graphs in Books: A Layout Problem with Applications to VLSI Design|journal = [[SIAM Journal on Algebraic and Discrete Methods]]|volume = 8|issue = 1|pages = 33–58| year = 1987 |last1 = Chung|first1 = F. R. K.|last2 = Leighton|first2 = F. T.|last3 = Rosenberg|first3 = A. L.|author-link1 = Fan Chung|author-link2 = Thomson Leighton|author-link3 = Arnold L. Rosenberg|doi = 10.1137/0608002|url = http://www.math.ucsd.edu/~fan/mypaps/fanpap/81books.pdf}}</ref> studied the problem of [[book embedding|embedding a graph into a book]] with the graph's vertices in a line along the spine of the book.  Its edges are drawn on separate pages in such a way that edges residing on the same page do not cross.  This problem abstracts layout problems arising in the routing of multilayer printed circuit boards.

[[Graph embedding]]s are also used to [[mathematical proof|prove]] structural results about graphs, via [[Minor (graph theory)|graph minor theory]] and the [[graph structure theorem]].
